2019B16.goal: In right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $C$), $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $BC$ satisfy $AC=CD$, $DE=EB$, and $AC:DE=4:3$. We want $AD:DB$. Two isosceles triangles hide a right angle at $D$, which unlocks the lengths.

tools.name: Base angles of an isosceles triangle
tools.fact: AC=CD\Rightarrow\angle CAD=\angle CDA;\quad DE=EB\Rightarrow\angle EDB=\angle EBD
tools.why: Equal sides face equal angles.

tools.name: Angles in a right triangle
tools.why: The right angle at $C$ uses up $90^\circ$ of the $180^\circ$.

tools.name: Pythagorean triple $3$-$4$-$5$
tools.why: Recognise the triple instead of computing.

tools.name: Coordinates for ratios on a segment
tools.why: A point on a segment is determined by the fraction of the way along it.

2019B16.approach: Name the angle at $B$ as $\beta$ and chase angles around $D$: the two isosceles triangles force $\angle CDE=90^\circ$. With $CD=4$ and $DE=3$, the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle gives $CE=5$, so $BC=CE+EB=8$. Then the whole triangle is known and $D$ is found by $CD=4$.

steps.title: Angle chase at $D$
steps.explain: Let $\angle B=\beta$, so $\angle A=90^\circ-\beta$. Since $AC=CD$, $\angle CDA=\angle A=90^\circ-\beta$. Since $DE=EB$, $\angle EDB=\beta$. The angles at $D$ along line $AB$ sum to $180^\circ$: $\angle CDE=180^\circ-(90^\circ-\beta)-\beta=90^\circ$.

check.q: If $\angle CDA=50^\circ$ and $\angle EDB=40^\circ$ on a straight line through $D$, what is $\angle CDE$?

steps.title: Find the side lengths
steps.explain: Scale so $AC=CD=4$ and $DE=EB=3$. Right triangle $CDE$ has legs $4,3$, so $CE=5$ and $BC=5+3=8$. Then $AB=\sqrt{4^2+8^2}=4\sqrt5$.

check.q: What is $\sqrt{4^2+8^2}$?
If $D$ is $\tfrac25$ of the way from $A$ to $B$, what is $AD:DB$?

2019B16.bridge: Chase angles to find the right angle at $D$, use $3$-$4$-$5$ to get $BC$, then locate $D$.
solution: With $\angle B=\beta$, the isosceles triangles give $\angle CDA=90^\circ-\beta$ and $\angle EDB=\beta$, so $\angle CDE=90^\circ$.
traps: Assuming $D$ is the foot of the altitude.
Forgetting that $BC=CE+EB$, not $CE$.
2019B16.recognize: Several isosceles triangles sharing a vertex on a line: chase base angles; the angles at that vertex often add to a right angle.

2019B17.goal: Two balls land independently in bin $k$ with probability $2^{-k}$. We want $P(\text{red}>\text{green})$. Symmetry between the two balls does most of the work once we know the chance they tie.

tools.name: Symmetry
tools.why: The two balls have identical, independent distributions.

tools.name: Complement
tools.why: Exactly one of the three happens.

tools.name: Geometric series
tools.why: Sum of an infinite geometric series with $|r|<1$.

2019B17.approach: Directly summing $P(R=j)P(G=k)$ over $j>k$ is a double series. Instead compute the easier event "same bin", then split the rest evenly by symmetry.

check.q: What is $\sum_{k\ge1}9^{-k}$?

steps.title: Use symmetry
steps.explain: The remaining probability $1-\tfrac13=\tfrac23$ splits equally between "red higher" and "green higher". So $P(R>G)=\tfrac13$.

check.q: If $P(\text{tie})=\tfrac25$ in a symmetric game, what is $P(\text{player 1 wins})$?

2019B17.bridge: Find the probability of a tie and split the rest evenly.
2019B17.shortcut: "Which of two identical independent quantities is bigger" is always $\tfrac12(1-P(\text{tie}))$.
traps: Answering $\tfrac12$ by forgetting ties.
Summing the double series and making an index error.
2019B17.recognize: Comparisons between two independent, identically distributed random values: compute the tie probability and use symmetry.

2019B18.goal: Henry repeatedly walks $\tfrac34$ of the way toward the gym (at $2$ km) or home (at $0$). In the long run he bounces between two points $A$ and $B$. We need $|A-B|$. The limiting points must be "fixed" by the walking rule.

tools.name: Moving a fraction of the way
tools.why: He covers three quarters of the remaining gap.

tools.name: Steady state (fixed points)
tools.why: In the limit, walking toward the gym from $a$ lands at $b$, and walking home from $b$ lands at $a$.

2019B18.approach: Do not follow the walk step by step. Assume it settles into bouncing between $a$ (near home) and $b$ (near the gym). Each must be what the rule produces from the other. That gives two linear equations.

steps.title: Write the rule
steps.explain: Walking $\tfrac34$ of the way from $x$ to the gym at $2$ lands at $\tfrac14x+\tfrac32$. Walking $\tfrac34$ of the way from $x$ toward home at $0$ lands at $\tfrac14x$.

check.q: From $1$ km, walking $\tfrac34$ of the way to the gym at $2$ km lands where?

steps.title: Solve for the limits
steps.explain: $a=\tfrac14b$ and $b=\tfrac14a+\tfrac32$. Substitute: $b=\tfrac1{16}b+\tfrac32$, so $\tfrac{15}{16}b=\tfrac32$, $b=\tfrac85$, and $a=\tfrac25$. So $|A-B|=\tfrac65$.

check.q: Solve $b=\tfrac1{16}b+\tfrac32$.

2019B18.bridge: Set up the two fixed-point equations and solve.
solution: Toward the gym from $x$: $\tfrac14x+\tfrac32$; toward home: $\tfrac14x$.
2019B18.shortcut: The gap shrinks to the fixed distance $d$ with $d=\tfrac34(2-a)-\ldots$; solving the pair of linear equations is fastest.
traps: Following many steps numerically and rounding.
Using $\tfrac34$ of the total distance $2$ each time instead of $\tfrac34$ of the remaining distance.
2019B18.recognize: "In the long run it oscillates between two points" or "approaches a value": write the equations the limit must satisfy instead of iterating.

2019B19.goal: $S$ is the set of divisors of $100000=2^55^5$. We count distinct numbers that equal a product of two different elements of $S$. Every such product has the form $2^a5^b$; we must find which exponent pairs are reachable.

tools.name: Divisors of $2^55^5$
tools.why: A divisor takes each prime to a power at most its power in $n$.

tools.name: Exponents add under multiplication
tools.why: Multiplying powers of the same base adds exponents.

tools.name: Counting by complement
tools.why: Products of any two divisors (allowing equal) give all $11\times11$ exponent pairs.

2019B19.approach: Allowing the two divisors to be equal, products give $2^a5^b$ with $0\le a,b\le10$: $121$ numbers. Then remove those that can only be made by multiplying a divisor by itself. That happens only at the extreme corners of the exponent grid.

steps.title: All products (equal allowed)
steps.explain: Any $0\le a,b\le10$ can be split as $a=x_1+x_2$, $b=y_1+y_2$ with each part between $0$ and $5$. So there are $11\cdot11=121$ products.

check.q: How many values of $a=x_1+x_2$ with $0\le x_i\le5$?

steps.title: Which need equal factors?
steps.explain: A pair $(a,b)$ needs $x_1=x_2$ and $y_1=y_2$ only if every split is forced to be equal. $a=0$ forces $0+0$; $a=10$ forces $5+5$; any other $a$ has a split with unequal parts. So the forced cases are $a\in\{0,10\}$ and $b\in\{0,10\}$: $1,\ 2^{10},\ 5^{10},\ 10^{10}$. That is $4$ numbers.

check.q: Can $2^{10}$ be written as a product of two distinct divisors of $2^55^5$?
What is $121-4$?

2019B19.bridge: Count all exponent pairs, then remove the four corners that force equal factors.
solution: Products of two divisors are $2^a5^b$ with $0\le a,b\le10$: $121$ possibilities.
Unless $a\in\{0,10\}$ and $b\in\{0,10\}$, there is a split into two distinct divisors.
The four corner values $1,2^{10},5^{10},10^{10}$ need equal factors.
2019B19.shortcut: Think of the exponent grid $0..10\times0..10$ and remove the corners.
traps: Removing all perfect squares (most squares have other factorizations, e.g. $2^2\cdot5^2=2^1\cdot2^15^2$).
Counting pairs of divisors instead of distinct products.
2019B19.recognize: Products of divisors: work with exponent vectors; sums of exponents form a grid, and only the extremes are forced.

2019B20.goal: A circle of radius $2$ centred at $F$ (the top of the middle semicircle) covers part of three unit semicircles on $AD$. The shaded region is inside the circle and outside the semicircles. We must express its area as $\tfrac ab\pi-\sqrt c+d$.

tools.name: Coordinates
tools.why: Placing $AD$ on the $x$-axis makes every circle easy to write.

tools.name: Sector area
tools.why: A sector is the fraction $\theta/360^\circ$ of the disc.

tools.name: Area by decomposition
tools.why: The middle semicircle lies entirely inside the circle, and each outer semicircle overlaps it in a region of area $X$.

2019B20.approach: The whole middle semicircle is inside the radius-$2$ circle (its farthest points $B,C$ are only $\sqrt2$ from $F$). The outer semicircles are only partly inside, so the work is finding $X$, the overlap of one outer semicircle with the circle. Note the circle passes through $E=(-2,1)$ and crosses $AD$ at $x=-\sqrt3$.

steps.title: Where the circle meets the left semicircle
steps.explain: The circle $x^2+(y-1)^2=4$ passes through $E=(-2,1)$ (top of the left semicircle) and meets the $x$-axis at $x=\pm\sqrt3$. The overlap $X$ is the quarter of the left semicircle to the right of $x=-2$ (area $\tfrac\pi4$) minus a small corner region $W$ near $(-2,0)$ that lies outside the big circle.

check.q: Where does $x^2+(y-1)^2=4$ meet the $x$-axis?

steps.title: Area of the corner region $W$
steps.explain: Take the rectangle $[-2,0]\times[0,1]$, area $2$. The part of the big disc inside it is a $30^\circ$ sector from $F$ (between directions to $E$ and to $(-\sqrt3,0)$), area $\tfrac{30}{360}\cdot4\pi=\tfrac\pi3$, plus the triangle $F,(-\sqrt3,0),(0,0)$, area $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$. So $W=2-\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ and $X=\tfrac\pi4-W=\tfrac{7\pi}{12}+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2-2$.

check.q: What is the area of a $30^\circ$ sector of a circle of radius $2$?

steps.title: Assemble
steps.explain: Shaded $=4\pi-\tfrac\pi2-2X=4\pi-\tfrac\pi2-\tfrac{7\pi}6-\sqrt3+4=\tfrac{7\pi}3-\sqrt3+4$. So $a+b+c+d=7+3+3+4=17$.

check.q: What is $4\pi-\tfrac\pi2-\tfrac{7\pi}{6}$?

2019B20.bridge: Subtract the middle semicircle and twice the overlap $X$ of an outer semicircle with the circle.
solution: Coordinates: $F=(0,1)$, circle $x^2+(y-1)^2=4$; the middle semicircle lies inside it.
The left semicircle's overlap is $X=\tfrac\pi4-W$, where $W=2-\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ is the corner of the rectangle $[-2,0]\times[0,1]$ outside the circle.
So $X=\tfrac{7\pi}{12}+\tfrac{\sqrt3}2-2$, and the right side is the same by symmetry.
2019B20.shortcut: Find where the big circle crosses the line through $E$ and $G$ (exactly at $E$ and $G$) and the $x$-axis ($\pm\sqrt3$); those points give the $30^\circ$ and $\sqrt3$ pieces.
traps: Assuming the outer semicircles lie entirely inside the circle.
Forgetting the part of the circle below $AD$, which is also shaded.
2019B20.recognize: Areas between overlapping circles: use coordinates to find intersection points, then build each piece from sectors and triangles.

2019B21.goal: Debra flips until she gets $HH$ or $TT$. We want the probability that she ends with $HH$ and she saw her second tail before her second head. With no two equal flips in a row before stopping, her flips alternate.

tools.name: Alternating sequences
tools.why: Any repeat ends the game.

tools.name: First-step equations
tools.why: Condition on the next flip and write the probability recursively.

2019B21.approach: For the second tail to come before the second head, the start must be $T,H,T$ (starting with $H$ would let the second head arrive first; $TT$ would end with tails). After $THT$ we need to eventually end with $HH$. Set up a small recursion for "ending with $HH$ from a position where the last flip was $T$".

steps.title: The forced start
steps.explain: The first flip must be $T$ (if it were $H$, the next head would be the second head before any second tail). Then $H$ (otherwise $TT$ ends with tails). Then $T$, so the second tail appears while there is only one head. Probability $\tfrac18$.

check.q: What is the probability the first three flips are exactly $T,H,T$?

steps.title: Recursion after a $T$
steps.explain: Let $p$ be the chance of eventually ending with $HH$ when the last flip was $T$. Next flip $T$: ends with $TT$ (fail). Next flip $H$: then $H$ again wins, or $T$ returns to the same state. So $p=\tfrac12\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac12p\right)$, giving $p=\tfrac13$.

check.q: Solve $p=\tfrac14+\tfrac14p$.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explain: $\tfrac18\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac1{24}$.

check.q: What is $\tfrac18\cdot\tfrac13$?

2019B21.bridge: Force the start $THT$, then use a one-state recursion for finishing with $HH$.
solution: From a state ending in $T$, let $p=P(\text{finish with }HH)$; $p=\tfrac12(\tfrac12+\tfrac12p)$, so $p=\tfrac13$.
2019B21.shortcut: After $THT$ the rest is $(HT)^kHH$ with probability $\sum_k(\tfrac14)^k\tfrac14=\tfrac13$.
traps: Allowing the sequence to start with $H$.
Forgetting that after $THT$ another $T$ ends the game with $TT$.
2019B21.recognize: Coin games that stop at a pattern: identify the forced prefix, then use first-step (Markov) equations for the rest.

2019B22.goal: Three players each start with $\$1$ and pass money at random each ring. We want the probability all three have $\$1$ after $2019$ rings. Only two kinds of states exist, which makes a tiny Markov chain.

tools.name: State reduction
tools.why: Money is conserved ($\$3$ total) and someone with $\$0$ cannot give.

tools.name: Transition probabilities
tools.why: Count the equally likely choices that lead back to everyone having $\$1$.

2019B22.approach: Find the probability of being at $(1,1,1)$ after the next ring from each state. If both give the same number, the history does not matter and the answer is that number.

steps.title: From $(1,1,1)$
steps.explain: Each of three players chooses one of two others: $8$ outcomes. Everyone ends with $\$1$ only if the gifts form a cycle ($A\to B\to C\to A$ or reverse): $2$ outcomes. Probability $\tfrac14$.

check.q: How many ways can three people each give to one of the other two?

steps.title: From $(2,1,0)$
steps.explain: Only the $\$2$ player and the $\$1$ player give: $4$ outcomes. They end at $(1,1,1)$ only if the rich player gives to the $\$1$ player and the $\$1$ player gives to the broke player: $1$ outcome. Probability $\tfrac14$.

check.q: With holdings $(2,1,0)$, how many equally likely giving outcomes are there?

steps.title: Conclude
steps.explain: Whatever the state before the last ring, the chance of ending at $(1,1,1)$ is $\tfrac14$. So after $2019$ rings the probability is $\tfrac14$.

check.q: If every state leads to state $X$ with probability $\tfrac14$, what is $P(X)$ after the next step?

2019B22.bridge: Reduce to two states and compute the chance of reaching $(1,1,1)$ from each.
solution: The only possible holdings are $(1,1,1)$ and permutations of $(2,1,0)$.
So after any ring the probability is $\tfrac14$. The answer is $\textbf{(B)}\ \tfrac14$.
2019B22.shortcut: When every state transitions to the target with the same probability, that probability is the answer for any number of steps.
traps: Trying to track $2019$ steps.
Letting the broke player give money.
2019B22.recognize: Long repeated random processes with few states: compute transition probabilities; often one step's structure decides everything.

2019B23.goal: Points $A$ and $B$ lie on a circle whose tangents at $A$ and $B$ meet on the $x$-axis. We need the circle's area, i.e. $r^2$.

tools.name: Equal tangents
tools.why: So $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

tools.name: Tangent ⟂ radius
tools.why: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

tools.name: Altitude to the hypotenuse
tools.why: In right triangle $PAO$ with altitude $AM$, the altitude squared equals the product of the hypotenuse pieces.

2019B23.approach: Find $P$ first: it is on the $x$-axis and on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. The centre $O$ is also on that bisector, and triangle $PAO$ has a right angle at $A$ with $M$ (midpoint of $AB$) the foot of the altitude. Then $r^2=AM^2+MO^2$.

steps.title: Find $P$
steps.explain: $M=(9,12)$, and $AB$ has slope $\tfrac{11-13}{12-6}=-\tfrac13$, so the bisector has slope $3$: $y-12=3(x-9)$. At $y=0$, $x=5$: $P=(5,0)$.

check.q: A line through $(9,12)$ with slope $3$ meets the $x$-axis where?

steps.title: Right triangle $PAO$
steps.explain: $PM=\sqrt{4^2+12^2}=\sqrt{160}$ and $AM=\tfrac12AB=\tfrac12\sqrt{40}=\sqrt{10}$. Since $\angle PAO=90^\circ$ and $AM\perp PO$: $AM^2=PM\cdot MO$, so $MO=\tfrac{10}{\sqrt{160}}$.

check.q: In a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse is $6$ and one piece is $4$. What is the other piece?

2019B23.bridge: Find $P$ on the bisector, then use the right triangle $PAO$ and its altitude $AM$.
solution: $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ ($y-12=3(x-9)$) and the $x$-axis: $P=(5,0)$.
$PM=\sqrt{160}$, $AM=\sqrt{10}$; triangle $PAO$ is right-angled at $A$ with altitude $AM$.
traps: Taking $P$ as the centre.
Using $AB$ instead of $AM=\tfrac12AB$.
2019B23.recognize: Two tangents from one point: the point, the centre and the chord's midpoint are collinear on the perpendicular bisector, and similar right triangles relate everything.

2019B24.goal: The sequence $x_{n+1}=\tfrac{x_n^2+5x_n+4}{x_n+6}$ starts at $5$ and decreases toward $4$. We need roughly how many steps until it is within $2^{-20}$ of $4$, only to choose an interval.

tools.name: Shift to the limit
tools.why: Subtracting the limit turns the recursion into a multiplication by a factor slightly below $1$.

tools.name: Geometric decay estimate
tools.why: For $0<y\le1$, the factor $\tfrac{y+9}{y+10}$ lies between $\tfrac9{10}$ and $\tfrac{10}{11}$.

tools.name: Logarithm estimate
tools.why: Solve $r^m=2^{-20}$ for $m$.

2019B24.approach: Find the limit ($4$) and study the distance $y_n=x_n-4$. The recursion becomes $y_{n+1}=y_n\cdot(\text{a factor near }0.9)$. Bound the factor above and below, so $y$ shrinks geometrically, and estimate how many multiplications reach $2^{-20}$.

check.q: Factor $x^2+x-20$.

steps.title: Bound the factor
steps.explain: $y_0=1$ and $y$ decreases, so $0<y\le1$ and the factor $\tfrac{y+9}{y+10}$ is between $\tfrac9{10}$ and $\tfrac{10}{11}$. So $(\tfrac9{10})^m\le y_m\le(\tfrac{10}{11})^m$.

check.q: For $y=1$, what is $\tfrac{y+9}{y+10}$?

steps.title: Estimate $m$
steps.explain: We need $y_m\le2^{-20}$. With ratio $\tfrac9{10}$: $m\ge\tfrac{20\ln2}{\ln(10/9)}\approx\tfrac{13.86}{0.105}\approx132$; with $\tfrac{10}{11}$: $m\le\tfrac{13.86}{0.0953}\approx146$ (plus one). Either way $m$ is in $[81,242]$.

check.q: Approximately, what is $\ln2$?

2019B24.bridge: Shift by the limit, bound the shrinking factor, and estimate the number of steps with logarithms.
solution: For $0<y\le1$ the factor is between $\tfrac9{10}$ and $\tfrac{10}{11}$.
Reaching $2^{-20}$ takes between about $132$ and $147$ steps.
2019B24.shortcut: Since $(0.9)^{7}\approx\tfrac12$, halving takes about $7$ steps, so $20$ halvings take about $140$ steps.
traps: Thinking convergence is fast (quadratic) like Newton's method.
Using $\log_{10}$ and $\ln$ inconsistently.
2019B24.recognize: Recursive sequences approaching a limit: subtract the limit and look at the ratio $y_{n+1}/y_n$; a ratio near a constant means geometric decay.

2019B25.goal: We count $0$–$1$ strings of length $19$ that start and end with $0$, have no $00$, and no $111$. Between consecutive $0$s there must be one or two $1$s, so the string is built from blocks.

tools.name: Block decomposition
tools.why: No $00$ means at least one $1$ between zeros; no $111$ means at most two.

tools.name: Counting arrangements of blocks
tools.why: Arrange $p$ blocks of one type and $q$ of another in a row.

2019B25.approach: After the first $0$, the rest of the string is a sequence of blocks "$10$" (length $2$) or "$110$" (length $3$) filling $18$ positions. Count solutions of $2p+3q=18$ and arrangements for each.

steps.title: Set up blocks
steps.explain: Write the string as $0$ followed by blocks, each block being $10$ or $110$ (ones then the next zero). The blocks fill the remaining $18$ characters, so $2p+3q=18$ with $p$ short and $q$ long blocks.

check.q: Which string uses blocks correctly after a leading $0$: $0\,10\,110$?
For $2p+3q=12$, which $(p,q)$ pairs work with $p,q\ge0$?
What is $\binom74$?

2019B25.bridge: Decompose into blocks $10$ and $110$, solve $2p+3q=18$, and count arrangements.
solution: After the initial $0$, the string is a sequence of blocks $10$ or $110$ totalling $18$ characters.
2019B25.shortcut: A recursion $a_n=a_{n-2}+a_{n-3}$ (Padovan-like) also works if you build up from short lengths.
traps: Forgetting the leading $0$ when counting length.
Allowing blocks of three $1$s.
2019B25.recognize: Strings with "no two/three in a row" constraints: split at a forced symbol into blocks of limited lengths, then count compositions.
